match.reason: The closest point, fiscal policy (e-fiscal), covers deliberate changes to spending and taxes, while automatic stabilisers are the narrower idea of taxes and welfare changing on their own, so no existing point is the same.

draft.title: Automatic stabilisers
card: Automatic stabilisers are features of the budget that change government spending and revenue as the economy changes. They work without any new decision by the government.
In a downturn, incomes and spending fall, so income tax and GST collected fall too. Households keep more of their income than they would under a fixed tax bill, which supports demand.
In a downturn, more people lose jobs and qualify for payments such as JobSeeker. Government spending rises, which supports household spending.
In a boom the effect reverses. Tax revenue rises and welfare spending falls, which takes some heat out of demand. The stabilisers soften swings in the business cycle but do not remove them.
draft.remember: Stabilisers act on their own: the budget leans against the cycle without a new policy decision.

a.q: Why does a downturn increase spending on unemployment payments without any new government decision?
opts: More people meet the existing rules to qualify for payments
Parliament passes a new stimulus package each time jobs fall
The Reserve Bank lowers the cash rate to fund the payments
Tax rates are cut automatically to make up for lost wages
a.why: Payment rules are already in place, so more people qualify as unemployment rises and spending goes up. A new stimulus package would be a discretionary decision, which is the opposite of an automatic stabiliser.
a.clue: The rules stay the same, but the number of people meeting them changes.

b.q: Australia's economy slows and many workers lose overtime and jobs. The government announces no new measures. What happens to the budget through automatic stabilisers?
opts: Tax revenue falls and welfare spending rises, easing the slump
Tax revenue rises and welfare spending falls, cooling demand
Tax revenue and welfare spending both fall as incomes drop
Nothing changes until the next Budget sets new tax rates
b.why: Lower incomes and spending mean less tax is collected, and more people claim welfare, so the budget supports demand without any new decision. Option two describes what happens in a boom, so it is the tempting reversal.
b.clue: Think about what happens to incomes, then to tax collected and to claims for payments.
